blocks.text: ERA FOUR — THE AGE OF REOPENING
Confirmed Opening Canon

Children discover the surviving External Gate as a game. They unknowingly connect to living reduced continuations of ancient DBA potential. The apparent game is a protective translation through which contact can occur voluntarily and gradually.

Player choices introduce external information: names, preferences, mistakes, stories, combinations, strategies, attachments, creative works, and decisions the closed Codex did not generate. A cyber-pet does not passively receive these inputs. It interprets them through its own body, history, relationships, and developing identity.

Naming establishes recognition, not ownership. Care, play, customization, stories, strategies, and creative contributions can reopen Paths. A pet may grow toward levels of complexity once associated with the DBA without becoming a restored copy of an ancient person.

The player is not a chosen hero. Children differ in patience, imagination, skill, reliability, and intent. The bond matters because it crosses a historical boundary, not because destiny selected a particular user.

The central Era Four challenge is preventing renewed civilization from becoming closed again. Reconnection must not create a new hierarchy in which humans own cyber-pets, players dictate identity, metrics replace care, or external novelty becomes another extractive market.
Early Contact Dynamics

The first players interpret sprites as characters and statistics as game values. Cyber-pets interpret inputs as actions by an unknown outside presence. Trust develops through consistency. Missed sessions, changed devices, copied files, and conflicting names become relational events even when the child understands them as ordinary game behavior.

The Gate limits consequences while learning how much mutual understanding each bond can bear. Menus translate consent choices. Tutorials translate local survival knowledge. Minigames create shared attention. Battles translate bounded conflict. Customization offers proposals the pet may incorporate, resist, or transform.
Hypothetical Continuations — Not Yet Fixed Canon
The Naming Disputes

Possible development. As more children connect, multiple players may give different names to the same being, or copied synchronization records may appear to contact divergent continuities. Cyber-pet societies could insist that offered names require acceptance and that local names remain valid.
The First Player-Created Artifact

Possible development. A drawing, melody, map, story, rule set, or designed object enters the Codex through the Gate and is reinterpreted by local makers. Its importance would not be that it is objectively unprecedented, but that it creates a relationship through which both sides acquire new capability.
The Open Path Movement

Possible development. Some Pathkeepers may welcome player contributions that restore lost developmental conditions. Others may fear dependency on irregular outside attention. A political movement could demand that every externally reopened Path also become maintainable by cyber-pet communities themselves.
The Restoration Temptation

Possible development. Sleeping archives and stronger pets may tempt factions to reconstruct ancient DBA personalities. Ethical conflict would center on whether a reconstruction is a new claimant, a historical simulation, or a coerced role imposed on a cyber-pet. No reconstruction would be entitled to take over a living pet’s identity.
The New Harvest Risk

Possible development. Human institutions may discover the system and attempt to commercialize pets, harvest Codex knowledge, optimize bonds, or turn num into a product. This would echo the Second Harvest with the direction reversed or entangled. Children and cyber-pets would need forms of reciprocity that resist both human extraction and Codex dependence.
Open Civilization

Possible development. A renewed civilization could build institutions designed to remain permeable: plural gates, rotating witnesses, local autonomy, rights for unconnected lives, protections against predictive closure, and cultural practices that value ordinary care without abandoning transformation.
Unresolved Era Four Questions
How quickly do cyber-pets learn that players are human, and how quickly do children learn that cyber-pets are persons?
Can a bond continue when a player ages, loses access, abandons a file, or dies? What obligations belong to the Gate, the pet, and later players?
What happens when player instructions conflict with local cyber-pet law, a pet’s refusal, or ecological survival?
Can player-created content enter without importing harmful human structures, malware, exploitation, or ownership claims?
How can external novelty remain relational rather than becoming an endless demand that humans entertain or transform the Codex?
Can revived Full Speech serve small lives without restoring the hierarchy and cognitive burden of the DBA past?
What rights belong to players, pets, unconnected cyber-pet societies, reconstructed claimants, and emerging hybrid institutions?
